newsitem.title: USA: Clinton pledges to help nation's capital.
newsitem.headline: Clinton pledges to help nation's capital.

text.p: President Bill Clinton Friday pledged to tackle the dire financial problems of the nation's capital in an effort to rescue the District of Columbia from what he called "a series of purgatories."
Clinton said the District's budgetary chaos stemmed from a confusing role as part city, part state in which it had to provide the services of both without the financial support of a state government.
"There's been too much of a gray area," Clinton said at a news conference. "It is not quite a state and not quite a city, not quite independent and not quite dependent."
"And very often, when responsibilities are divided, they end up being nobody's responsibility."
As a result, the District had found itself in a series of budgetary "purgatories" over the years, Clinton said.
"We have to try to resolve this, and I promise you a more serious effort," he added.
Clinton said he was impressed with the strategic plan for the city developed by a five-member board appointed by Congress in 1995 to oversee the District's finances.

But he did not address the board's request that the federal government take over about $1 billion worth of the city's programs that are typically paid for by states. His spokesman Mike McCurry said problems with the city's management made a huge injection of federal money unlikely.

The board's plan, released Thursday, said the District would not emerge from mounting financial crisis unless the U.S. government took over funding such programs as Medicaid, mental health care, prisons and road maintenance. Cities usually pass those costs on to their states.
Clinton said he was awaiting further details from the Office of Management and Budget and the D.C. Control Board on how to proceed.
"I want to think in a larger way -- what kind of systematic efforts we can make to be constructive in the revitalization of Washington," Clinton said.
He urged inhabitants of other cities to appreciate tthe capital's dilemma. "The American people need to understand the unique challenges facing Washington," Clinton said.
Behind its tourist attractions -- the White House, the monuments and the museums -- Washington is a troubled city with a rapidly declining population of 570,000, many poor and black.
For most of its history the 10-mile-square enclave that came to be called the District of Columbia was controlled by the federal government and Congress.
However, in 1974 Congress relinquished that power, awarded the District financial independence -- or home rule -- and the right to vote for a mayor and city council.
The city is in dire financial straits with a bloated bureaucracy, crumbling services and a collapsing school system.

The District faces a budget shortfall of $85 million this year which must be met through aggressive cuts in spending and personnel. But the city already is short of fire trucks and emergency vehicles. Police cars go unrepaired, potholes unfilled, crime flourishes and a U.S. general was recently appointed by the board to run its schools.
In a recent example of the city's crime problems, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ruth Ginsberg was mugged outside her home.
The city's drinking water supply is also poor, polluted at times by bacteria growth in aging pipes and seepage from leaking sewer lines.
Mayor Marion Barry said Friday he was "delighted" to hear the president address Washington's problems.
"He seems to be saying that he wants Washinton treated like other world capitals," Barry said. "The national government has to see us as a unique situation -- a crown jewel -- and has to support us."
